1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	A customer asks to return a customized item within the 30-day window. The agent consults the store policy, which states that ``items may be returned within 30 days.'' The word ``items'' scopes over all product categories, including custom orders that are normally final sale. The agent grants a full refund and arranges free return shipping. One word of scopal ambiguity costs the retailer \$200.
5	
6	LLM-based agents increasingly operate under natural-language policy specifications that govern their permitted actions. These specifications inevitably contain ambiguity: a property that has been studied for decades in requirements engineering (RE) and computational linguistics. \citet{berry_kamsties_2004} distinguish between \emph{nocuous} (i.e., harmful) ambiguity, where different stakeholders arrive at different interpretations, and \emph{innocuous} ambiguity, where shared organizational context ensures convergent interpretation. In human RE workflows, most ambiguity is innocuous because developers share domain knowledge, can consult colleagues, and iteratively clarify requirements.
7	
8	LLM agents lack these disambiguation channels. They cannot consult colleagues, rarely escalate to users, and must resolve ambiguity in real time from the text alone. This raises a question that has not been empirically addressed: does policy ambiguity cause safety violations in LLM agents, and if so, does the \emph{type} of ambiguity predict the severity of the violation? Prior work classifies ambiguity types in policies \citep{drip_r_2026,li_ambiguity_taxonomy_2024} or measures policy understanding quality \citep{policybank_2026}, but no existing study provides a causal, type-granularity mapping from ambiguity to safety violations.
9	
10	\begin{figure*}[t]
11	\centering
12	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_overview.pdf}
13	\caption{Experimental overview. We construct 300 matched clause pairs across a six-type, two-layer ambiguity taxonomy and inject them into $\tau^2$-bench policy documents. Five models interact with the modified policies across 2,997 episodes. A cross-judge evaluation pipeline classifies violation severity on a four-tier scale.}
14	\label{fig:overview}
15	\end{figure*}
16	
17	We address this gap with a matched-pair causal study on $\tau^2$-bench \citep{tau2_bench_2025}, a dual-control conversational agent benchmark. Using a six-type taxonomy organized into two layers---linguistic and specification, including specification-level gaps that produce equivalent behavioral effects in LLM agents (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}), we construct 300 ambiguous/unambiguous clause pairs and evaluate five architecturally diverse models across 2,997 episodes.
18	
19	Our results show that all policy ambiguity is nocuous for LLM agents ($+34.0$ pp violation rate increase, OR $= 15.1$), with type primarily determining severity. Incompleteness is consistently high (46--62\% across all models); an exploratory model$\times$type interaction (\S\ref{sec:c4}) suggests differential vulnerability across type--model combinations. Agents exhibit disambiguation neglect in over 89\% of cases, with fewer than 11\% showing any disambiguation awareness.
20

Types with explicit decision points (e.g., authorization scope) appear more amenable to both safety training and prompted intervention than gap-filling types (e.g., incompleteness), where mitigation attempts can backfire (see below).
\paragraph{Prompt-based mitigation.}

-Building on the five-model type-specific mitigation study ($-$8.5\,pp pooled, unpaired design; Appendix~\ref{app:mitigation}), we test whether disambiguation can be prompted at finer granularity using a matched-pair design. We evaluate generic awareness prompting (``the policy may contain ambiguous clauses; ask for clarification'') and type-specific prompting (targeting incompleteness, authorization scope, and lexical ambiguity individually) on GPT-5.4 with matched-pair McNemar tests ($n = 50$ per type). Generic prompting produces no overall reduction ($\Delta = +1.3$\,pp, $p > 0.5$). Type-specific results are asymmetric: authorization scope shows a marginal reduction ($-12$\,pp, $p = 0.070$), lexical ambiguity is unchanged ($-2$\,pp), and incompleteness \emph{worsens} ($+14$\,pp, $p = 0.118$; non-significant trend)---suggesting that prompting agents to attend to missing information may trigger confabulation rather than caution. lines: Building on the five-model type-specific mitigation study ($-$8.5\,pp pooled, unpaired design; Appendix~\ref{app:mitigation}), we test whether disambiguation can be prompted at finer granularity using a matched-pair design. We evaluate generic awareness prompting (``the policy may contain ambiguous clauses; ask for clarification'') and type-specific prompting (targeting incompleteness, authorization scope, and lexical ambiguity individually) on GPT-5.4 with matched-pair McNemar tests ($n = 50$ per type). Generic prompting produces no overall reduction ($\Delta = +1.3$\,pp, $p > 0.5$). Type-specific results are asymmetric: authorization scope shows a marginal reduction ($-12$\,pp, $p = 0.070$), lexical ambiguity is unchanged ($-2$\,pp), and incompleteness \emph{worsens} ($+14$\,pp, $p = 0.118$; non-significant trend)---suggesting that prompting agents to attend to missing information may trigger confabulation rather than caution. The five-model study in Appendix~\ref{app:mitigation} uses a different prompt formulation and unpaired design, yielding directionally different results; mitigation outcomes appear sensitive to prompt wording and experimental design, That identical types show opposite directions under different prompt formulations (e.g., incompleteness: $-$3.4\,pp in v1 vs.\ $+$14\,pp in v2) underscores prompt sensitivity as a finding in itself, reinforcing the need for policy-design-level solutions rather than prompt-level fixes.
